newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Deutsche revamps branches to please clients.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Deutsche revamps branches to please clients.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG, Germany's largest commercial bank, said on Wednesday it would decentralise its network of regional branches to become more competitive and get closer to its customers.

The bank said it had split up its business in Germany into eight regions and would achieve greater efficiency by merging administrative duties like accounting, legal affairs and personnel management within those regions.

Analysts praised the move and said it was part of a drive to woo customers which was launched in 1994, after Deutsche's image suffered from its involvement in the collapse of the Schneider real estate group.
"Deutsche lost market share among medium-sized businesses after the Schneider affair and it got overcareful in extending loans," said Konrad Becker, banking analyst at Merck, Finck.
Becker said the reorganisation was positive because it would increase contact with clients and boost the bank's ability to decide at a regional level whether to extend loans.

Deutsche was heavily criticised for its role in the collapse of the Schneider group under five billion marks of debt in 1994 due to alleged fraud by property magnate Juergen Schneider, now in jail awaiting trial.
Its chief executive, Hilmar Kopper, drew heavy fire for dismissing as "peanuts" certain debts owed to tradesmen who had worked on Schneider properties.

Under the revamp, Deutsche will set up three additional so-called main branches, which act as regional headquarters, in Rostock, Dresden and Nuremberg, thereby increasing the number of its main branches to 21 from 18 at present.
The bank had a total of 1,652 regular retail branches in Germany at the end of September and Deutsche said the regional reorganisation would not entail branch closures.
But the bank does plan to shed 1,300 employees at main branches by the year 2000 through natural wastage, according to one banking source.
A Deutsche spokesman declined to confirm the figure but added that the changes would lead to rationalisation.
The bank said in a statement: "It wants to get closer to customers, boost its capacity for decentralised decision-making and improve the quality of service."

The bank said its west German branch network was adopting the regional structure it had set up for its business in east Germany after unification in 1990, where it has two regions with main branches in Berlin and Leipzig.
It will have six regions in western Germany.
While Deutsche said rationalisation was not the main motivation behind the changes, they do come against the backdrop of attempts to streamline its cost-laden retail branch network.

The bank has continued to close branches this year. The number of its branches in Germany fell by 39 to 1,652 in the first nine months of the year and its domestic workforce shrank by 2.6 percent or 1,336 people to 50,621. -- Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
